definition: Too focused on small details or rules, often in a way that shows off knowledge.
example: The tour guide's pedantic asides about dates and spellings lost the attention of the whole group.
nuance: Meticulous praises careful attention, but pedantic criticizes it as showy fussing over points too minor to matter.
prompt: You are telling a funny story to friends at lunch when one of them speaks up.
options: My pedantic friend stopped my joke to note that a spider is not technically an insect.
The pedantic joke was so ordinary and dull that nobody at the lunch table bothered to laugh.
My pedantic friend never cares about accuracy and lets every small mistake slide by.
Everyone praised how pedantic my timing was, since the punch line landed perfectly.
reasons: Interrupting a joke over a trivial technical point is the kind of fussiness the word criticizes.
Dull and ordinary fits the look-alike pedestrian; this word is about nitpicking, not blandness.
Shrugging off errors is the reverse of fixating on them.
The word is a criticism of fussiness, so it cannot serve as praise for good comic timing.

practice.prompt: A student reviews a classmate's poster before the science fair opens.
options: The pedantic reviewer insisted on fixing a comma that no visitor would ever notice.
The poster's pedantic design used plain fonts and a familiar layout seen at every fair.
Being pedantic, the reviewer skimmed the poster in seconds and said any errors were fine.
The pedantic reviewer warmly urged the classmate to trust her bold, big-picture ideas.
reasons: Demanding a correction nobody would care about shows excessive concern with minor rules.
Plain and unoriginal describes something pedestrian, not something fussy about details.
A quick glance that waves away mistakes is the opposite of nitpicking.
Encouraging broad ideas has nothing to do with an irritating focus on small points.
